persons.name: John Foot
persons.note: THE 1835 POLL LIST AND A SECOND INDEPENDENT SOURCE. Read from poll_1835, tax_1833. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G1a), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. tax_1833 stands against this person's name by 31 December 1833 and nothing says when they came. THE 1833 TAX LIST IS A PROPERTY ROLL, NOT A RESIDENCE CHECK (T-1117): it names the owner of ground inside the town, resident or not, and its own entry 110 is a man three years dead. It bounds the town's RECORD of this name and not the day this person reached Chicago. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the town's own paper carries this name by 1 July 1835; whether the man it names was standing in the town is a claim this record cannot make, and present_on_scene_date says `uncertain` for that reason. No figure is drawn (L1). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 2 times: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Foot, John” (tax_1833_030, line 82); Poll list of 1835 — “Foot, John” (poll_1835_024, line 309). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Foot' agrees with the entry's forenames; 2 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 2 times, as “FOOT JOHN”, 1833-10-22: 2 parcels of the school section — lot 5 of block 117 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E); lot 6 of block 117 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), 0.00 acres stated in all, for $190.00 (ls0153, ls0154). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: FOOT JOHN matches John Foot: the forename names John Foot of the 2 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. FERGUS 1839'S FORT DEARBORN ADDITION LOT SALE — JUNE 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. This person bid at the sale of the Fort Dearborn Addition, 10-24 June 1839, printed in Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 at pages 47-49. The bidder is printed as “John Foot”. 1 lot row, $152 in all: block 4 lot 44 at $152 (f1839_lot0064, printed page 47). The sale table's own shorthand, recorded and not flattened: 1 carries the block number forward from the last row that printed one. What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago between the 10th and the 24th of June 1839 and bid at the Fort Dearborn Addition sale. It is written as 1839 evidence with describes_date 1839-06, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a land sale four years after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. THE LOT IS NOT A LOCATION FOR 1835: the Fort Dearborn Addition is the Beaubien, or Reservation, lands, which in July 1835 were the garrison's ground and were not platted into lots at all. It places no house, no shop and no household in the town this project builds. No trade, no address in the town of 1835, no household and no house. persons.name: Benjamin Jones
persons.note: APPOINTED THE TOWN'S FIRST STREET COMMISSIONER ON 7 NOVEMBER 1833 and resigned before his term expired: Andreas, 'It was during these days that Benjamin Jones was appointed Street Commissioner, but on account of ill-health resigned before his term expired, and was succeeded by O. Morrison and Silas W. Sherman.' His health is the only medical fact about any private resident in this parcel. The Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 is the only contemporary Chicago document this project holds; an advertiser in it was paying to be found, which makes it strong evidence of existence and address in November 1833 and weak evidence of survival to 1 July 1835, nineteen months and about 2,400 people later. OLD SETTLERS, 1882 — A DATE OF DEATH, AND NOTHING ABOUT 1835. John Wentworth's roll of old settlers who had died since 1 January 1881, kept for the Calumet Club and printed in the Chicago Tribune of 25 April 1882, carries “Benjamin Jones, Aug. 11, 1881.”. That corroborates a Chicago residence before 1840 and fixes the END of this life, which this record did not carry; it is not an arrival and it places nobody in the town on 1 July 1835. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: T-0513 consolidates the identity and T-0515 regrades. Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (data/research/old_settlers/crosswalk.json). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Jones, Benjamin” (poll_1834_060, line 229). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Jones' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 5 times, as “JONES BENJAMIN”, 1833-10-22 to 1836-06-22: 1 lot in the platted town — lot 7 of block 35 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L7BL35CHIOT, as printed) and 4 parcels of the school section — BL121 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; lot 2 of block 117 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E); lot 4 of block 23 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E); lot 4 of block 80 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), 0.00 acres stated in all, for $7133.00 (ls0254, ls0255, ls0256, ls0257, ls1263). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $6000.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: JONES BENJAMIN matches Benjamin Jones: the forename names Benjamin Jones of the 6 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. No figure is drawn (L1). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the city register of 1839 — “John A. Nelson” as sheriff of cook county, 1864 (f1839_r0104, printed page 39). What a match may carry, and it depends on WHICH TABLE it landed in. A match on printed page 38, or on any row of the mayors' table, is 1839-or-later evidence: it says the man held that office in that year and was therefore in Chicago in that year, it is written with the row's own describes_date and never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on it alone — a later appearance is corroboration of CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not of July 1835. A match on the sheriffs' rows of 1831, 1832, 1834 or 1836 is different in kind: the office is contemporary with the town, the 1834 row's term covers the scene date outright, and such a match carries reaches_scene. Even there the SOURCE is a retrospect — a table running to 1874, set in 1876 out of Old Settlers' recollections per the compiler's warning on printed page 3 — so it may be cited as a contemporary office and may not be graded `documented` without a second, nearer record. The ward on printed page 38 is a ward of the CITY of 1839 and places no house in the town of 1835. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Nelson' folds to the same string as the register entry's, and the given name of both begins J. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Nelson, Miss Jane | Profession. | September 30, 1870. | Dismissed.” (second_presb_0765, printed page 196), admitted 1870-09-30 by profession. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Nelson' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins J. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with T-0515, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

persons.name: Thomas Jefferson Vance Owen
persons.note: BORN IN KENTUCKY, 5 APRIL 1801, AND DIED AT CHICAGO ON 15 OCTOBER 1835 - fifteen weeks after the scene date, which is why this household is one of the few in the dataset whose presence on 1 July 1835 is settled at both ends. Andreas, scan p. 195: 'Colonel Owen was born in Kentucky, April 5, 1801. He was appointed Indian agent in the winter of 1830-31, but did not arrive in Chicago until the spring of 1831 ... When the Town of Chicago was incorporated in 1833, Colonel Owen was chosen President of its first board of trustees. He died at Chicago, October 15, 1835.' THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago, 10 August 1833 — “Owen, Col. T. J. V.” (poll_1833_021, line 42). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Owen' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 4 times, as “OWEN THOMAS J V”, 1833-10-23 to 1833-10-24: 4 parcels of the school section — BL105 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; BL108 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; lot 1 of block 84 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E); lot 3 of block 23 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), 8.72 acres stated in all, for $676.00 (ls0297, ls0298, ls0299, ls0300). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: OWEN THOMAS J V matches Thomas Jefferson Vance Owen: the forename names Thomas Jefferson Vance Owen of the 2 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

residents.research_note: THE TOWN'S FIRST PRESIDENT AND THE UNITED STATES' AGENT TO THE POTAWATOMI, IN THE LAST SUMMER OF HIS LIFE. Two things make this a good anchor record. The first is that the presence question is closed at both ends: an arrival in the spring of 1831 and a death at Chicago on 15 October 1835, both in Andreas. The second is that the household is the dataset's first demonstration of the honest failure mode - one named person and an unnamed remainder that the record refuses to invent. THE RECORD DELIBERATELY DOES NOT CARRY OWEN'S ROLE IN THE 1833 TREATY AS AN OCCUPATION. He signed as a commissioner for the United States at the treaty of 26 September 1833 that ceded the land this town stands on, and that is a fact about the removal rather than about a trade; it is recorded here in prose and the household is flagged for review because of it.
